samples.text:
The bar chart shows the percentage of people in different age groups in one country who shopped online every week in 2015 and 2025.

In 2015, the 25–34 age group had the highest percentage with 38%. The 16–24 group was 31% and the 35–49 group was 29%. Older people shopped online less. Only 16% of people aged 50–64 and 5% of people over 65 was shopping online weekly.

In 2025, all of the age groups increased. The 25–34 group was still the highest, it rose to 68%. The 35–49 group more than doubled to 61%, so it was higher than the 16–24 group, which only reach 52%. The biggest change was in the older groups. The 50–64 group went up to 47%, almost three times more than before, and the over 65 group rose from 5% to 32%.

Overall, online shopping become more popular in every age group, and the young adults aged 25–34 shopped online the most in both year. Older people were the least, but they increased quickly.
samples.why: Figures accurate with some relevant comparison · overview present but placed last · linking simple and repetitive · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, tense and punctuation errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares the proportion of people in five age groups in a particular country who made online purchases at least weekly in 2015 and 2025.

Overall, weekly online shopping became considerably more common among all age groups over the decade. People aged 25–34 were the most frequent online shoppers in both years, whereas those aged 65 and over were the least, although the older groups saw the most rapid growth.

In 2015, 38% of 25–34-year-olds shopped online every week, slightly more than the 16–24 and 35–49 groups, at 31% and 29% respectively. Participation was much lower among older people, with just 16% of those aged 50–64 and only 5% of the over-65s doing so.

By 2025, the figure for the 25–34 group had increased by 30 percentage points to 68%. The 35–49 age group more than doubled its share to 61%, overtaking the youngest group, which rose more modestly to 52%. The most striking growth, however, occurred among older people: the proportion of 50–64-year-olds almost tripled to 47%, and the figure for those over 65 went up more than six times, reaching 32%.
samples.why: Clear overview of overall growth and the narrowing gap · key features well highlighted · logical progression with good linking · some less common expressions · mostly accurate with one or two awkward phrasings.

samples.text:
The chart shows the percentage of people in five age brackets in one country who shopped online at least once a week in 2015, compared with 2025.

The habit of weekly online shopping spread across every age group over the ten years. The 25–34 group remained the most active throughout, but the gap between younger and older shoppers narrowed considerably, as the steepest proportional rises were among the over-50s.

In 2015, weekly online shopping was concentrated among those aged under 50, with rates ranging from 29% in the 35–49 group to 38% among 25–34-year-olds. The figures for older people were far lower: 16% for the 50–64 group and a mere 5% for those aged 65 and above.

A decade later, the 25–34 group still led, with more than two-thirds (68%) shopping online weekly. The 35–49 age group had more than doubled its rate to 61%, overtaking 16–24-year-olds, whose participation grew by a comparatively modest 21 points to 52%. Meanwhile, the proportion of 50–64-year-olds nearly tripled to 47%, and the over-65s recorded the most remarkable change of all, rising more than sixfold from 5% to 32%.
samples.why: Skilful selection of key features, including relative growth · clear overview · accurate figures and derived comparisons · cohesion well managed · precise, varied vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
